title: Analytic properties of cross-click operators in passive multi-basis photodetection: monotonicity, exact convergence rates, and dimension reduction for quantum key distribution
abstract: Cross-click operators, the POVM elements for simultaneous clicks in detectors assigned to different measurement bases, are used in QKD and entanglement-verification analyses with realistic threshold detectors to bound multiphoton contributions. Earlier applications verified the needed growth of the minimum eigenvalue $f^{(n)}$ on the $n$-photon subspace only numerically over finite sectors. This work gives an analytic characterization for passive linear-optical analyzers with arbitrary efficiency mismatch and dark counts. The key observation is that every silence operator is the second quantization $Γ(A)$ of an explicit single-photon contraction $A$, whose $n$-photon restriction is $A^{\otimes n}$ on $\mathrm{Sym}^n$. This yields: (i) monotonicity $f^{(n+1)}\ge f^{(n)}$; (ii) two-sided exponential bounds $\max_b γ_b|A_b|^n \le 1-f^{(n)} \le \sum_b γ_b|A_b|^n$, which determine the exact asymptotic convergence rate from single-photon spectral data; (iii) for ideal detectors and $n\ge1$, the exact formula $f^{(n)}=1-\sum_b p_b^n$; and (iv) an exact factorization $1-f^{(n_A,n_B)}=(1-f_A^{(n_A)})(1-f_B^{(n_B)})$ for the two-party cross-click operator. The results apply to polarization, time-bin, and spatial-mode analyzers within the stated threshold-detector model. As an application, we obtain closed-form photon-number weight bounds used in detection-efficiency-mismatch analyses, replacing finite-sector Fock-space numerics by formulas valid for all photon numbers.
summary: This paper analytically characterizes the behavior of cross-click operators essential for bounding multiphoton contributions in QKD security proofs. By showing these operators are related to second quantization structures, the authors derive monotonicity and exact exponential convergence rates. These results replace complex Fock-space numerics with general formulas applicable to any passive linear-optical analyzer.
main_problem: The paper aims to provide a sharp analytic characterization of cross-click operators used in security analyses for Quantum Key Distribution (QKD) when using realistic, lossy photodetection detectors.
main_result: It establishes monotonicity ($f^{(n+1)}\ge f^{(n)}$), derives two-sided exponential bounds determining the exact asymptotic convergence rate, and provides an exact factorization for joint cross-click operators.
method: The core method involves relating the 'silence' operator to the second quantization of an explicit single-photon contraction, allowing the derivation of spectral properties from finite-dimensional matrix inequalities.
model_or_system: The system models passive multi-basis photodetection using linear optics followed by threshold detectors characterized by arbitrary efficiencies and dark counts. The analysis is performed on the infinite-dimensional Fock space.
key_observables: Cross-click operators (POVM elements), minimum eigenvalue $f^{(n)}$ of the cross-click operator on the $n$-photon subspace, and joint surface $f(n_A, n_B)$.
important_parameters: Detector efficiencies ($\eta_d$), dark-count probabilities ($\epsilon_d$), and the number of photons ($n$).
main_assumptions: The results assume independent dark counts and uncorrelated detection efficiencies; they are derived for any passive analyzer structure.
figures_summary: Figure 1 illustrates a running example using a six-state polarization analyzer. Figure 2 shows $f(n)$ under varying efficiency mismatches, while Figure 3 displays the joint surface $f(n_A, n_B)$ as an exact formula.
paper_structure: The paper builds from defining the cross-click operator using POVMs to establishing structural theorems: first proving monotonicity (Theorem 1), then deriving two-sided exponential bounds and the convergence rate (Theorem 2), followed by specific results for ideal detectors and joint operators (Corollaries/Theorem 3).
why_interesting: This work provides rigorous, closed-form analytical tools to analyze fundamental security limitations in quantum communication protocols that previously required computationally intensive numerical simulations.
